items.summary: A spokesman for Afghanistan's interior ministry says the blast was caused by carelessness at an explosives depot nearby.
items.body:

ByJacob Phillips

At least seven students have been killed and 99 others have been injured following an explosion near a school in Afghanistan, an official has said.

The incident happened on Saturday morning in the Anderseir area of Asadabad, the capital of Kunar province, a spokesperson for the Taliban government's interior ministry said.

Posting on X, Abdul Mateen Qani said that according to initial investigations, the blast was caused by "negligence and carelessness" at an explosives depot belonging to nearby mining companies.

An investigation into the incident was ongoing, he added.

items.title: OpenAI counter-sues Apple over alleged theft of trade secrets
items.summary: The ChatGPT-maker alleges that tech giant Apple stole trade secrets through a former employee.
items.body:
Image source, Reuters

ByAmy Walker

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has counter-sued Apple, alleging that the iPhone maker stole trade secrets through a former employee.

In a federal lawsuit filed in July, Apple sued the artificial intelligence (AI) company and two of its employees who previously worked for Apple, claiming it had engaged in a "pattern of theft" of proprietary information.

A countersuit, filed in California on Friday, alleged that Apple gained confidential information through the hiring of a former OpenAI employee and accuses it of discouraging hardware suppliers from working on future OpenAI devices.

Apple denied the counterclaims, describing them as "a transparent attempt to distract from the substance" of its own case.

OpenAI is developing AI-enabled personal devices, which it claims in the countersuit could threaten to "outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf".

The filing alleged Apple had gained confidential information by rehiring a former employee who had worked at OpenAI for six months.

OpenAI accused the employee, who it said gained access to information on a new device and the company's roadmap for future physical products, of sending "dozens of OpenAI documents" to his personal phone numbers. It also said he presented OpenAI's plans to senior Apple staff "at Apple's request".

OpenAI said: "Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place."

The counterclaim also alleged Apple encourages employees to mix work files with their personal iCloud (Apple's cloud storage service) accounts so it could later accuse those who leave to work for competitors of theft.

A spokesperson for Apple said: "This case is about OpenAI employees deliberately stealing, accessing, and using Apple's secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products - not about inadvertent retention of Apple information."

In its own lawsuit, the tech giant alleged that at least two long-time Apple workers who left the company to join OpenAI took part in a "pattern of theft" by emailing themselves internal Apple information.

Apple also accused the AI firm of undertaking a "strategy to extract Apple's confidential information".

A spokesperson for OpenAI previously denied the claims, telling the BBC: "We have no interest in other companies' trade secrets."

Along with OpenAI, and two former Apple employees, Apple is also suing io Products, the design startup founded by Sir Jony Ive, a long-time Apple executive who designed the iMac, iPod, iPhone and iPad.

OpenAI acquired the company last year in a $6.5bn (£4.7bn) deal.

items.title: Explosion at a school in eastern Afghanistan kills 7, wounds more than 90
items.summary: Local officials said the blast appeared to have originated in a neighboring depot for mining explosives.
items.body:
Middle East

Explosion at a school in eastern Afghanistan kills 7, wounds more than 90

November 28, 20266:32 AM ET

By

The Associated Press

This is a locator map for Afghanistan with its capital, Kabul.

AP Photo/AP

hide caption

AP Photo/AP

KABUL, Afghanistan — An explosion at a school in the eastern Afghan province of Kunar Saturday killed seven people and wounded more than 90, the province's culture and information director said, adding that the blast appeared to have originated in a neighboring depot for explosives.

Sami ul Haq Bayan said initial information indicated the blast at the school on the outskirts of the provincial capital, Asadabad, occurred due to negligence at the depot storing explosives belonging to mining companies. An investigation into the incident was underway, he said.

Up to 15 of the wounded remain in hospital, while the rest were discharged after treatment, he added.

Earlier, Kunar Provincial Police Headquarters spokesperson Farid Dehqan said the explosion occurred at 10 a.m. at a school in the Andar Ser area on the outskirts of Asadabad.

Footage posted on social media showed cars bringing wounded children to the emergency department of a hospital in Asadabad, as well as images of the school building, part of which appeared to have collapsed.

Mining is a major industry in Afghanistan, a country that is rich in raw materials, including iron ore, copper, lead, zinc, gold, coal and precious stones. But safety standards at the mining companies are often poor, leading to accidents.

Gemstone mining is on the rise in Kunar, with various companies extracting precious stones which are subsequently sold at auction.

In August, a hand grenade attack at a school complex in the Afghan capital, Kabul, wounded more than 40 children aged between 9 and 14.

items.title: As Spain votes, what could change for Europe?
items.summary: Spain votes on Sunday. A loss for Pedro Sanchez and a shift to the right in Madrid could affect how one of the EU's largest countries approaches migration, defense and the war in Gaza.
items.body:

Recent polls have predicted a tight race, putting the conservative People's Party (PP) and the Socialists led by Pedro Sanchez (above) neck and neckImage: Francisco Seco/AP Photo/picture alliance

Advertisement

Walking through the halls of the European institutions in Brussels these days, it feels as if people are whispering about the end of an era. What happens when one of the most vocal leaders of Europe's center left is no longer at the table?

Pedro Sanchez is one of the few social democratic prime ministers left in the European Union, and Spain is the largest member state still led by one. That's why this election raises questions that go beyond who governs in Madrid.

After more than eight years in office Sanchez called a snap election at the beginning of October, three days after parliament rejected two emergency decrees aimed at tackling Spain's housing crisis. Anger over soaring housing costs has brought protesters onto the streets nationwide this year.

On November 11, protesters took part in nationwide general strike over the country's housing crisisImage: Thomas Coex/AFP

Sanchez's minority government was already under pressure over its handling of the summer migration crisis in Ceuta and accusations of corruption against his party and his wife, which both he and his wife have denied.

Polls on Monday predicted a tight race, putting the conservative People's Party (PP) at around 32% and the Socialists led by Sanchez at 31%.

With the right-wing populist Vox party in third place at around 17%, the polling projected an absolute majority for the PP and Vox combined. The two parties would still have to decide whether they want to govern together.

Alberto Nunez Feijoo leads the opposition People's Party, and could be Spain's next prime ministerImage: Juan Medina/REUTERS

Important center-left voice may be 'silenced'

A change of government in Madrid would cost Europe's center left one of its most influential voices, Javier Carbonell, a policy analyst at the European Policy Centre in Brussels, told DW. "This voice might now be silenced."

Carbonell said three positions have set Sanchez apart: his willingness to challenge US President Donald Trump, his support for Palestinian statehood and his defense of immigration into Europe. Sanchez has been one of the few EU leaders who have continued to argue that migrant workers help fill labor shortages, support an aging Spanish and European population and sustain growth.

Could Spain's train disaster upend Sanchez's election campaign?

Earlier this year, his government opened a program to grant legal status to eligible migrants already living in Spain. It received more than 1 million applications. Spain's economy grew by 2.6% last year, nearly double the eurozone average, and the government expects GDP to grow by 2.6% this year and 2.2% in 2027.

Will Spain take a tougher line on migration?

The conservative PP has campaigned for tighter immigration controls while keeping routes open for workers in sectors facing shortages. Vox wants sharper cuts to immigration, more deportations and an end to regularization for new arrivals. It also wants Spanish citizens to get priority for subsidized housing and other social benefits.

This stance is nothing new at the European level. "With a PP-Vox government, Spain would join the general European trend towards an anti-immigration policy," said Carbonell, adding that he could see Madrid moving closer to countries pushing for tougher return policies. Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands are already in talks with Rwanda about setting up a hub for people whose asylum claims have been rejected.

Camino Mortera-Martinez, an associate fellow at the Centre for European Reform, agrees that a shift in Madrid would reinforce a trend already underway in Europe. "This anti-migration tendency doesn't come from European leaders, but from voters," she told DW.

How the far right hardened Europe's migration stance

PP, Vox back higher defense spending

Another domain where Spain could potentially change course and influence its European neighbors concerns its defense policies. Spain raised defense spending from 1.24% of GDP in 2024 to 2% in 2025, reaching NATO's previous benchmark.

Nevertheless, Sanchez has pushed back against the alliance's new annual target of 5% of GDP by 2035, which includes both military spending and broader security investments. He has argued that Spain could meet its NATO capability commitments by spending around 2.1% of GDP.

Both the PP and Vox favor higher defense investment but leave the exact figure open in their election programs. "They have a voting base that has no problem to increase defense spending, contrary to Sanchez," said Mortera-Martinez.

A shift on Israel and Palestinian statehood?

Mortera-Martinez also expects a change in Spain's approach to the Middle East, should Sanchez lose the election.

"The current government has been at the forefront of defending the last bastions of international and public law," she said.

Spain formally recognized a Palestinian state in May 2024. Sanchez has accused European leaders of applying double standards by rallying behind Ukraine against Russia's invasion, while failing to defend international law with the same resolve in the Middle East. In April, he pushed to suspend the EU's agreement with Israel, which makes respect for human rights an essential part of the relationship.

Carbonell, too, believes a new conservative government would be less vocal in its support for the Palestinians. "Sanchez was able to influence people on the subject matter, moving the consensus a bit more towards pro-Palestine," he said.

If Sanchez comes up short on Sunday, Europe's social democrats would lose their strongest foothold among the EU's largest countries. But, said Carbonell, a defeat in Spain could reignite a debate across the European center left about how to win back voters and stay politically relevant elsewhere.

RIYADH: Saudi Arabia said on Saturday (Nov 28) it shot down a cruise missile targeting the capital Riyadh, after Houthi media reported Saudi strikes on Yemen.

A Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government has been regularly bombing areas controlled by the Iran-backed group since Yemen's civil war reignited over the summer.

items.title: Two staff killed in Israeli strike on Gaza medical clinic, MSF says
items.summary: The Israeli military says it targeted "Hamas terrorists" in the strike which has been condemned by the World Health Organization.
items.body:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Médecins Sans Frontières says the number of its staff who have been killed in Gaza has risen to 17

ByJames Chater and Rushdi Abualouf, Gaza correspondent

Updated 31 minutes ago

Two workers for the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) have been killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza, according to the organisation.

MSF said the strike was a direct hit on one of the charity's clinics, the location of which was known by the Israeli military.

In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the two people were Hamas operatives "acting as security guards at a clinic operated by MSF". The IDF added the strike was "not directed at a hospital" and caused no damage to medical infrastructure.

The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) said that attacks on health facilities and health workers in Gaza were "outrageous and unacceptable".

In a post on X, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote: "Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked."

In its statement, MSF - which is also known as Doctors Without Borders - said that the two workers who were killed were watchmen, and added that the strike brought the number of its colleagues killed in Gaza to 17.

The organisation said it was "devastated and outraged" and added: "​Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military."

In its own post on X, the IDF said that the two men, who they named as Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, were "terrorists in Hamas' military wing".

The Israeli military added it was another example of Hamas "embedding itself within international organizations".

It said that "precautionary measures were taken to minimize harm to civilians" before the strike on Gaza City, adding the men had "advanced plans to carry out attacks against Israeli civilians & IDF troops".

Witnesses told the BBC the two men were sitting at the clinic entrance when an Israeli drone descended and fired a missile.

Video footage from the scene of the strike showed a small crater beside a plastic chair, with bloodstains and limited damage in a courtyard behind the medical clinic.

Hundreds of Palestinians have since attended the funeral of the MSF workers, carrying the two bodies, wrapped in white plastic bags and placed on stretchers, on their shoulders as they made their way through the streets of the city.

Mohammed Imad, a close friend of Abu Hasira, one of the men killed, said he had seen him just hours before the attack.

"He was a peaceful, kind-hearted man. His only concern was looking after his wife, his two children and his mother," he told the BBC.

He said Abu Hasira had no affiliation with any armed group and had worked at the clinic for a long time.

The two workers' deaths follow an increase in Israeli strikes across Gaza over the past week.

Gaza's civil defence spokesman said eight Palestinians were killed in Israeli attacks across the Strip during the day, including the two MSF workers.

Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under the control of Hamas, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.

At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to tens of thousands of shelters for displaced families.

The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,770 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

A staff member of the medical charity Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) stands at the entrance of a clinic run by the organisation after two men working as security guards for the charity were killed on Friday in an Israeli airstrike that struck a building inside an MSF clinic compound in Gaza City on Nov 28, 2026. JERUSALEM: Doctors Without Borders (MSF) said on Saturday (Nov 28) an Israeli strike killed two staff members at a clinic in Gaza, with the Israeli army labelling the pair as Hamas "terrorists".

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) identified the men, who worked as security guards at the clinic, as Ahmad Abou Hassira and Hamas artillery cell commander Moaz Sobh.

MSF said it was "devastated" by the killings and denounced "a direct hit" on the organisation.

"Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military," it wrote on X.

World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus slammed the attack.

"Attacks on health facilities, health workers and humanitarian personnel in #Gaza are outrageous and unacceptable," he posted on X.

The IDF denied targeting a hospital or damaging medical infrastructure.

"This is another example of the Hamas terrorist organization embedding itself within international organizations," it posted on Telegram.

The US military repelled a half dozen drones swarming Britain's RAF Lakenheath base earlier this month, the Financial Times reported on Saturday (Nov 28), saying Iran was suspected of being linked to the incident.

The newspaper, citing people familiar with the matter, said the US deployed counter-drone technology to repel the unmanned aerial systems but that the drones were not retrieved by British or American personnel.

Asked for comment on the report, a spokesperson for the UK's Ministry of Defence told Reuters in an emailed statement: "Ministry of Defence Police and Suffolk Police worked closely with USAF Security Forces to respond to reports of unauthorised drone activity at RAF Lakenheath on 13 Nov and the situation was quickly resolved, with RAF Lakenheath returning to normal security and force protection measures."

The White House and Pentagon did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

In the incident, US Air Force personnel at the base responded to "suspected unauthorised drone activity", and an Air Force spokesperson said at the time that no personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected.

In a September incident at RAF Fairford, another British base used by the US Air Force, a threat linked to Iran prompted the removal of American B-1 bombers, President Donald Trump said last month.

Tehran has rejected accusations of involvement in the Fairford incident or other malign activity in Britain, where the authorities have for years accused Iran of being involved in plots and attempted assassinations against dissidents and Israeli and Jewish targets.

items.summary: Ukraine also reported hundreds of Russian drones fired at several regions, with one person killed and five injured.

World

Russia says shot down more than 1,200 Ukraine drones overnight

Ukraine also reported hundreds of Russian drones fired at several regions, with one person killed and five injured.

A Russian drone falls down after it was intercepted by a Ukrainian air defence unit amid Russia's attack on Ukraine in Kyiv on Nov 25, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Vladyslav Sodel)

FAST

MOSCOW: Russian authorities said on Saturday (Nov 28) that more than 1,200 Ukrainian drones had been shot down in a new night-time attack, with hundreds aimed at the Moscow region.

Ukraine also reported hundreds of Russian drones fired at several regions, with one person killed and five injured. Both sides have stepped up air attacks in recent months.

More than 460 drones headed towards the Moscow area between late Friday and early Saturday, the capital's mayor Sergei Sobyanin wrote on the state-backed Max platform. He added that 123 were destroyed as they neared the city.

The Russian defence ministry said that air defence forces "intercepted and destroyed 1,246 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles" in more than a dozen regions including Moscow.

The Russian capital is about 500 kilometres from the nearest section of the Ukraine border. Other regions cited by the ministry, including Volgograd and Krasnodar, are also hundreds of kilometres from Ukraine.

Ukraine also reported widespread new attacks.

Ivan Fedorov, head of the Zaporizhzhia military administration, said Saturday that more than 700 Russian drones had been fired at the region over the past 24 hours, with one person killed and five injured. Russia's defence ministry said it had attacked military-linked targets.

Attacks have become more entrenched as the war closes in on its fifth anniversary. US efforts to mediate an end to hostilities have failed to reach any accord, except for prisoner exchanges.

items.title: Australian wrestler Bronson Reed dies aged 38, WWE says
items.summary: Tributes have flooded in for the 38-year-old Australian who is survived by his pregnant wife, Paige, their daughter.
items.body:
Image source, WWE via Getty Images

ByJessica Lamb

Professional wrestler Bronson Reed has died aged 38, World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE) has announced.

The company said the wrestler, whose real name is Jermaine Haley, died on Friday due to medical complications but did not give further details.

Paying tribute, WWE added: "Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague."

They also offered condolences to the Australian's family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, and their daughter.

WWE has been contacted for further comment.

Haley was honoured at the WWE event at Akins Ford Arena in Athens, Georgia on Friday.

The show began with a 10-bell salute for Haley and in his match, Canadian wrestler Kevin Owens wore an armband that read "Bronson" and addressed the crowd.

Owens said Haley loved performing.

"I knew for a fact, beyond performing in this ring, he loved his family more than anything so tonight if there is anything to take away from a tragedy like that - it's take care of each other and love each other... Forgive each other," Owens said.

"Bronson, for me, we were lucky to have you and you will be extremely missed."

WWE greats posted tributes online including the retired 16-time world champion Ric Flair, who wrote: "another soldier in our business that left us way too early!"

WWE Hall of Famer Diamond Dallas Page said "I was deeply saddened to read about the passing of Bronson Reed. I couldn't help but think of Eddie. Such a shame. My heart goes out to his friends & family. RIP brother."

WWE wrestler Eddie Guerrero - known as Latino Heat - died of heart failure at age 38 in 2005.

Image source, WWE via Getty Images

Image caption,

Bronson Reed in action against Dragon Lee during RAW in New York in November.

Australian pro wrestler Brendan Vink, who goes by Duke Hanson, posted "I love you, Jermaine." on X.

According to wrestling media outlets, Haley had recently been recovering from injuries sustained during the WWE Crown Jewel event in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia earlier in November.

He did not have a match during the event but was tossed off the stage and through a set of tables during a brawl.

Haley initially competed around the independent wrestling scene as Jonah Rock and J-Rock before signing with WWE in 2019.

He was released in 2021 before returning a year and continuing with WWE up until his death. In 2024, he won the André the Giant Memorial Battle Royal.

Haley is the second wrestler to die in the last few months after Benjamin Satterley, an English wrestling star passed away at the age of 40 in September.

No cause of death was provided at the time.

items.title: Indian workers fill Germany's labor gaps but face hurdles and risks
items.summary: The number of Indians working in Germany has grown rapidly in recent years. But many continue to face challenges in the labor market. Some also fall victim to recruitment scams, leaving them vulnerable to exploitation.
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5Pyc6

Prefer DW on Google

Germany, facing a shrinking and rapidly aging population, is seeking skilled professionals in a number of sectors Image: Gunter Hübner/dpa/picture-alliance

Advertisement

Pratyay Saikia was studying food technology in 2022 when he saw an advertisement from Magic Billion, a recruitment agency that places skilled and semi-skilled Indian professionals in verified jobs abroad.

The 25-year-old from the northern Indian state of Haryana reached out to explore employment opportunities.

Four years later, he is working as a butcher at Metzgerei Lederer in southern Germany, having completed a three-year apprenticeship at the butcher shop.

"I came to Baden-Württemberg with 180 other Indians who came here to do an Ausbildung [apprenticeship] program. Me and seven others did our Ausbildung at Lederer [butcher shop], while others went into the construction sector. I now have a full-time job here," Saikia told DW.

He is not alone as the number of Indian workers subject to social security contributions in Germany has grown sevenfold over the past decade, to over 140,000 professionals.

Many of them work in the IT and health care sectors.

India meets German engineering

Pressing need for workers, but hesitant to hire

Germany, facing a shrinking and rapidly aging population, doesn't just need software specialists and nurses. It is also seeking skilled professionals such as electricians, mechatronics technicians, solar panel installers and truck drivers.

A 2024 study by Bertelsmann Foundation concluded that Germany needs 288,000 foreign skilled workers per year until 2040 to fill the shortage left by retiring workers. Another report from the consulting firm FMC Group noted that over 369,000 skilled job positions went unfilled in 2025.

Despite the pressing need for skilled workers, many firms, particularly Germany's renowned Mittelstand (small and medium-sized enterprises), are reluctant to recruit from places like India, say observers.

"Hiring an electrician from India is a relatively new concept for German companies, so they are hesitant," said Daniel Raja, managing director of NM NextMittelstand GmbH, a Düsseldorf-based recruitment firm focused on connecting German firms with skilled workers from India.

The Mittelstand companies are often overlooked by young talent abroad, while many of these firms are not actively recruiting international skilled workers, Raja said.

This disconnect, coupled with the often high German language requirements, means that many skilled positions remain unfilled, he explained.

Germany looks to India to address skilled labor shortage

Language a key hurdle

Saikia, the butcher, had studied German to the B1 level, considered intermediate proficiency. He soon realized it was not enough for everyday communication at work.

"Initially, I found the theory classes of my Ausbildung quite difficult. But my co-workers helped me. After one year, my German improved, and I realized integration happened automatically as my language level improved," he said.

David Kipp, researcher in the Global Issues Research Group at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), said he's "skeptical" about lowering language requirements.

"Language skills are an important selection criterion so people actually know where they are going. Sending people with very little language knowledge makes exploitation easier, because they have less direct contact with German institutions," he told DW.

Language, however, isn't the only hurdle.

Raja said workers' councils also often resist hiring from abroad.

"Company decisions in the Mittelstand involve the team and the shop floor," he pointed out. "In some cases, the workers' council resists hiring from India because they mistakenly believe 'cheap Indian labor' will take their jobs or undercut their wages."

Raja said he often uses unconventional outreach methods, including hosting TikTok Live sessions, to engage directly with industrial employers and workers and dispel concerns and misconceptions.

Delivered! — The courier driver business

Exploiting the EU mobility loophole?

German companies have traditionally relied on workers from Central and Eastern European (CEE) nations such as Poland, Romania and Slovenia to fill labor market gaps.

But studies show CEE workers are increasingly reluctant to relocate to Germany, as faster economic growth and stronger career prospects improve opportunities in their home countries.

The situation has prompted recruitment agencies in these countries to look beyond the European Union for workers.

These third-country nationals (TCNs) obtain residence permits in CEE states and are then posted to German job sites under the Vander Elst visa. The mechanism allows non-EU citizens legally employed in one EU member state to be temporarily sent to work in another.

"European Labour Authority's (ELA) 2025 study on the posting of third-country nationals found that the number of posted TCNs is increasing. The main sectors concerned are construction and transport," said Pia Fallstrom, ELA spokesperson.

The exact number of TCNs posted across the EU is difficult to gauge, as data exchange between sending and receiving countries by nationality and sector is limited.

"Finding out how blue-collar workers get here really requires fieldwork," said Kipp, noting that Indian recruiters are aware of this mobility loophole and take advantage of these opportunities.

While there are regulations to protect workers posted to Germany from another EU state, ELA said the practice has often led to wage-dumping.

"ELA's work has identified issues such as difficulties accessing information on applicable rules, complex subcontracting arrangements, letterbox companies, bogus self-employment and other cases of non-compliance," noted Fallstrom.

"Posted third-country nationals can be particularly vulnerable because they may also depend on their employer for their work and residence permits."

Cost of a dream: Indian students in Germany

Raja said he had seen cases of workers falling victim to recruitment scams and being exploited as a result.

"I know of a family that took out a loan so that their child could enroll in an institute which promised a job in Germany," said Raja. "When the candidate realized it's a scam, they ended up in Bahrain doing a tough manual labor job just to pay off the loan."

What to do to prevent exploitative hiring practices?

Saikia, the butcher, stressed the importance of workers verifying that a recruitment agency is legitimate.

In his case, he said the agency's detailed website and its CEO's willingness to speak with him during the early stages of the recruitment process gave him confidence that it was not a scam.

Kipp, the SWP expert, argued that preventing exploitative hiring practices requires streamlining migration procedures, expanding pre-departure cultural training and becoming more effective at identifying trusted entities and combating social media scams.

"India is the most important country for experimenting with how work migration functions. If we don't pay attention, we'll just send people into the low-wage sector and into disappointment," he said.

"Finding out how blue-collar workers get here really requires fieldwork," said Kipp, noting that Indian recruiters are aware of this mobility loophole and take advantage of these opportunities.
While there are regulations to protect workers posted to Germany from another EU state, ELA said the practice has often led to wage-dumping.

"ELA's work has identified issues such as difficulties accessing information on applicable rules, complex subcontracting arrangements, letterbox companies, bogus self-employment and other cases of non-compliance," noted Fallstrom.
"Posted third-country nationals can be particularly vulnerable because they may also depend on their employer for their work and residence permits."

Raja said he had seen cases of workers falling victim to recruitment scams and being exploited as a result.

"I know of a family that took out a loan so that their child could enroll in an institute which promised a job in Germany," said Raja. "When the candidate realized it's a scam, they ended up in Bahrain doing a tough manual labor job just to pay off the loan."
What to do to prevent exploitative hiring practices?
Saikia, the butcher, stressed the importance of workers verifying that a recruitment agency is legitimate.
In his case, he said the agency's detailed website and its CEO's willingness to speak with him during the early stages of the recruitment process gave him confidence that it was not a scam.

Kipp, the SWP expert, argued that preventing exploitative hiring practices requires streamlining migration procedures, expanding pre-departure cultural training and becoming more effective at identifying trusted entities and combating social media scams.
"India is the most important country for experimenting with how work migration functions. If we don't pay attention, we'll just send people into the low-wage sector and into disappointment," he said.

items.title: Eight killed in Peruvian military helicopter crash
items.summary: The pilot was the sole survivor of the crash during a rescue mission in a remote area known for drug trafficking.
items.body:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

A Peruvian military helicopter crashed during a rescue mission

ByJessica Lamb

Eight military personnel have been killed in a helicopter crash in a remote area of Peru known for growing and trafficking drugs.

Authorities say the aircraft came down near the town of Sanabamba during a mission to evacuate an army patrol in the valley of the Apurimac, Ene, and Mantaro rivers, known by its Spanish acronym VRAEM.

Often referred to as 'Cocaine Valley', the area is Peru's largest coca-growing valley where gangs and the remnants of the former Shining Path rebel group operate.

The Peruvian ministry of defence said the pilot was the sole survivor of the crash, the cause of which is still unknown.

In its statement, the ministry said "search and rescue operations located the aircraft and the nine military personnel who were on board".

It named the pilot as Enzo Espinoza Roque and said he was evacuated to Lima to "receive specialised medical treatment".

The aircraft was reported missing on Thursday night after rescuing three army personnel.

No further information was shared about why the group needed to be rescued, but it was confirmed that they were among those who were killed in the crash.

Joint Command of the Peruvian Armed Forces posted a tribute online extending "deepest condolences to the family members, friends, and comrades-in-arms of the members of our VRAEM Special Command who lost their lives while carrying out a military mission. May God keep them in His glory".

In February, a MI-17 helicopter crashed in southern Peru in February killing all 15 on board.

Peru, along with Colombia, is one of the world's largest producers of coca leaves and cocaine, according to the United Nations.

items.title: Turkish officials 'destroyed' pro-opposition TV channel, owner tells BBC
items.summary: The headquarters of Halk TV were raided last month, the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed critical of the government.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Cafer Mahiroğlu says Halk TV has been "destroyed" by Turkish authorities

ByHarry Sekulich

Turkish authorities have "destroyed" one of the country's most-watched news channels, its London-based owner has told the BBC.

Speaking to the BBC's Newshour, Cafer Mahiroğlu said that nine people connected to Halk TV were arrested this week on charges including money laundering, bribery and spreading misleading information.

Mahiroğlu said that several of his family members were among those arrested when the pro-opposition channel was taken into government control last month, adding that the allegations against him and Halk TV are "completely wrong".

The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor' Office said that two former news anchors of the channel were among the most recent group of people detained.

In a statement, prosecutors accused the anchors of producing "false reports" in exchange for money.

Authorities have also issued an arrest warrant for the channel's news coordinator Kürşad Oğuz who is "abroad", the statement said, without specifying where.

Mahiroğlu told the BBC that he could be sent to prison if he tried to return to Turkey.

"[The government] wants to be in control of the whole media... I'm more worried about my country and my democracy than my channel," he said.

The headquarters of Halk TV was raided by Turkish authorities last month, halting the channel's live broadcasts, the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed to be critical of Turkish President Tayyip Erdoğan and his administration.

The government subsequently appointed a new administrator to run the channel.

Erdoğan's government controls much of the country's media, which ranks among the worst globally for press freedom, external, though the government insists that it does not detain media workers for carrying out journalistic activities.

However, the president has scaled up a crackdown on dissent since his narrow victory in the 2023 presidential election.

Earlier this month, authorities took control of pro-opposition network Sozcu TV.

Erdoğan's main challenger, mayor of Istanbul Ekrem Imamoğlu, has been jailed on corruption charges and for violating election laws, which he and his party have fiercely denied.

Hundreds of Imamoğlu's supporters have faced similar accusations, while the government has also imprisoned other campaigners, lawyers and comedians.

土耳其当局已“摧毁”该国收视率最高的新闻频道之一，该频道驻伦敦的所有者告诉BBC。

马希罗格鲁称，上个月这家亲反对派频道被政府接管时，他的几名家庭成员也在被捕者之列，并补充说针对他和Halk TV的指控“完全错误”。

伊斯坦布尔首席检察官办公室表示，该频道两名前新闻主播在最新一批被拘留人员之列。

检察官在一份声明中指控这些主播收受金钱制作“虚假报道”。

声明称，当局还对该频道的新闻协调员屈尔沙德·奥乌兹发出逮捕令，此人“身在国外”，但未说明具体地点。

马希罗格鲁告诉BBC，如果他试图返回土耳其，可能会被送进监狱。

“（政府）想要控制整个媒体……比起我的频道，我更担心我的国家和我的民主，”他说。

上个月，土耳其当局突袭了Halk TV总部，中断了该频道的直播，这是对被视为批评土耳其总统塔伊普·埃尔多安及其政府的新闻来源进行的一系列打压中的最新一起。

政府随后任命了一名新管理员来运营该频道。

埃尔多安政府控制着该国大部分媒体，土耳其的新闻自由在全球排名中位居最差之列，尽管政府坚称不会因媒体工作者从事新闻活动而拘留他们。

本月早些时候，当局接管了亲反对派网络Sozcu TV。

埃尔多安的主要挑战者、伊斯坦布尔市长埃克雷姆·伊马姆奥卢因腐败指控和违反选举法而被监禁，他和他的政党对此予以坚决否认。

数百名伊马姆奥卢的支持者面临类似指控，政府还监禁了其他活动人士、律师和喜剧演员。

items.title: Nigeria's acting legend who was loved across Africa and beyond
items.summary: Before becoming a household name in the Nigerian film industry, Edochie built a career in broadcasting.
items.body:
Image source, Supplied via Leo Edochie / Instagram

ByMansur Abubakar, Reporting fromAbuja and Wycliffe Muia, Reporting fromNairobi

For generations of Nigerians, Pete Edochie was more than a celebrated actor.

He was Okonkwo – the fierce, proud and troubled warrior whose portrayal in Things Fall Apart made him a household name and earned him a place in the hearts of millions.

Even in death, many Nigerians still refer to him by the character's name, a testament to the enduring impact of a role that defined his career.

Edochie died on 25 November, aged 79, in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.

In 1987, Edochie starred in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel. His portrayal of Okonkwo would change his life, establishing him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors and bringing him international recognition.

The series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.

Joy Nnamdi, a fan of both the novel and its television adaptation, believes Edochie was the perfect choice for the lead role.

She said nobody else could have brought the character to life as convincingly.

"His character Okonkwo gave a face to the highly celebrated novel," she told the BBC in Nigeria's biggest city, Lagos.

The role also cemented his reputation as a hard man, a screen persona he would maintain through much of his career.

"It was very rare to see him laugh in movies. He was the ultimate tough man," Nnamdi added.

With his deep, authoritative voice, imposing presence and effortless command of African proverbs, Edochie had a way of dominating a scene without raising his voice.

Whether playing a village elder, a wealthy businessman or a feared traditional ruler, he became an enduring embodiment of patriarchal authority on screen.

Edochie went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has grown into one of the world's largest.

From Kenya to South Africa, MultiChoice's Africa Magic channels helped take his films into millions of African homes as Nollywood became a cultural phenomenon across the continent.

Although many of his films were rooted in his Igbo culture, their themes of family loyalty, inheritance disputes, spiritual beliefs and the abuse of power resonated with audiences far beyond Nigeria.

Before becoming a household name in the film industry, however, Edochie had built a successful career in broadcasting.

Born on 7 March 1947 in Zaria, northern Nigeria, he attended primary and secondary school in Kaduna before studying journalism and television at the School of Journalism and Television in the UK.

He joined the Eastern Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation in 1967, the year Nigeria's civil war broke out.

He joined the pro-separatist Voice of Biafra, and recently described the war years as the greatest personal challenge he ever faced.

"During the war, the experience that we had as Biafrans, you know, survival was difficult. Hunger was driving us into eating all sorts of nonsense," he recalled.

He rose through the ranks to hold senior management positions but then switched to acting. Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals and Billionaire's Club.

Image source, T.E.N. / MPM via Netflix

Image caption,

Pete Edochie starred in Netflix's first original Nigerian film, Lionheart

His career also bridged the transition from home-video productions to global streaming platforms.

The 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart, which became Netflix's first original Nigerian film, introduced his work to a wider international audience.

He also worked in Ghana, where he starred alongside some of the country's biggest film stars in the 2017 comedy John and John.

His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).

He also received several other accolades, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.

In recent years, Edochie found an unexpected new audience online.

His distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films became popular social media memes, introducing his work to a younger generation of Africans.

For many who had never watched Things Fall Apart or his early Nollywood films, his stern expressions became a humorous way of conveying disbelief, disapproval or exasperation at everyday situations.

But his reputation as a formidable screen presence was no joke to those who grew up watching him.

Sani Muazu recalls that parents in the northern Nigerian city of Kano would sometimes invoke Edochie's name to keep misbehaving children in check.

"They would tell you: 'Okonkwo will come and visit you if you don't stop' and we would begin acting right," he said.

"To be honest, we grew up scared of him. Even though he was on the screen and not physically present, some of his roles added to our fears because he played some popular occultic roles, and villain roles suited him."

Image source, T.E.N. / MPM via Netflix

Image caption,

Edochie's expressions were sometimes used as online memes

Tributes poured in from fans and fellow actors following news of his death, with many describing him as a giant who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.

Popular actress Genevieve Nnaji paid her tribute in a post on X.

"I will let the assurance of the fact that you are a chosen one; and therefore, have returned to the most high God override my grief and heartbreak. May the heart of a true lion forever rest in peace. We love you," she wrote.

Patience Ozokwor, popularly known as Mama G, who appeared alongside Edochie in several productions, remembered him as a brilliant actor and a source of wisdom.

"He has been a father to stories that are told, like an elder sitting down telling you how things were done in those days," she told BBC News Pidgin.

"I called him any time, any day. He'll tell you what to do and what not to do."

Film director Babangida Bangis told the BBC that Edochie's death was a loss not just for Nigeria or Africa, but for the global film industry.

"Just days ago, during a seminar for filmmakers across the country, his name popped up as an example of brilliance on the screen, longevity and professionalism," he said.

"I think his loss is one for the world, not just Nigeria or Africa. We all grew up watching and loving him."

Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu also mourned the veteran actor, describing his death as a major loss to the country's film industry and cultural heritage.

The president, like many admirers, singled out Edochie's portrayal of Okonkwo, saying the performance and his subsequent roles had established him as one of Nigeria's most accomplished actors.

But beyond the fame and formidable character he portrayed on screen, his family remembers a man whose greatest legacy was the importance he placed on honesty and speaking the truth.

Leo Edochie, his son, told the BBC that his father was a strong-willed man.

"Of all his legacies, I think the whole world would agree that these two were the most important: telling the truth and remaining honest," he said.

He described his father as a man who lived an exemplary life, offering a model that young people could learn from and aspire to follow.

"I don't really have a choice, but the truth is that I have to carry on that legacy for our family," he added.

Edochie's influence also extended to his family, with two of his six children, Yul and Linc Edochie, following him into the Nigerian film industry.

Yet, for an actor so closely associated with stern expressions and intimidating characters, some of his most endearing moments came when he let his guard down.

In 2021, he made a brief appearance in music star Phyno's video for the song Highway, surprising fans with a display of dance moves that showed a lighter, more playful side of the septuagenarian.

It was a refreshing reminder that the man behind the formidable screen persona could also laugh, dance and enjoy himself.

"I will let the assurance of the fact that you are a chosen one; and therefore, have returned to the most high God override my grief and heartbreak. May the heart of a true lion forever rest in peace. We love you," she wrote.
Patience Ozokwor, popularly known as Mama G, who appeared alongside Edochie in several productions, remembered him as a brilliant actor and a source of wisdom.
"He has been a father to stories that are told, like an elder sitting down telling you how things were done in those days," she told BBC News Pidgin.
"I called him any time, any day. He'll tell you what to do and what not to do."
Film director Babangida Bangis told the BBC that Edochie's death was a loss not just for Nigeria or Africa, but for the global film industry.
"Just days ago, during a seminar for filmmakers across the country, his name popped up as an example of brilliance on the screen, longevity and professionalism," he said.
"I think his loss is one for the world, not just Nigeria or Africa. We all grew up watching and loving him."
Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu also mourned the veteran actor, describing his death as a major loss to the country's film industry and cultural heritage.
The president, like many admirers, singled out Edochie's portrayal of Okonkwo, saying the performance and his subsequent roles had established him as one of Nigeria's most accomplished actors.
But beyond the fame and formidable character he portrayed on screen, his family remembers a man whose greatest legacy was the importance he placed on honesty and speaking the truth.
Leo Edochie, his son, told the BBC that his father was a strong-willed man.
"Of all his legacies, I think the whole world would agree that these two were the most important: telling the truth and remaining honest," he said.
He described his father as a man who lived an exemplary life, offering a model that young people could learn from and aspire to follow.
"I don't really have a choice, but the truth is that I have to carry on that legacy for our family," he added.
Edochie's influence also extended to his family, with two of his six children, Yul and Linc Edochie, following him into the Nigerian film industry.
Yet, for an actor so closely associated with stern expressions and intimidating characters, some of his most endearing moments came when he let his guard down.
In 2021, he made a brief appearance in music star Phyno's video for the song Highway, surprising fans with a display of dance moves that showed a lighter, more playful side of the septuagenarian.
It was a refreshing reminder that the man behind the formidable screen persona could also laugh, dance and enjoy himself.

items.title: 'Poison seller' Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims
items.summary: The Canadian man, who pleaded guilty to 14 counts of aiding and abetting suicide earlier this year, said he was remorseful for his actions.
items.body:
Image source, PA Media

ByBrandon Drenon

Canadian prosecutors are seeking a 25-year prison sentence for a man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries.

Kenneth Law pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.

The 61-year-old will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.

During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.

If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.

As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".

"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.

She also said Law's motives were financial.

"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.

Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for many of their battles with mental illness.

He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims.

"Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place."

Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.

The sentencing hearing on Friday followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.

Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.

Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.
